## 5. EOD REFRESH HOOK

Dashboard *data* is refreshed by scheduled tasks, not by the server:
- **`AlphaQuant Daily Review`** (16:10 ET) → `run_daily_review.bat` → `generate_daily_review.py` calls `full_daily_review_html(..., regenerate_narrative=True)`, which **regenerates and caches the LLM narrative** for the day and writes `outputs/reports/daily_review_latest.html`. This is what keeps `/daily-review-v2`'s cached narrative current.
- **`AlphaQuant_EodReconciliation`** (16:50 ET) → 3 actions: `eod_reconciliation.py`, `eod_debrief.py` (writes `outputs/reports/eod_debrief_&lt;date&gt;.md`, the canonical round-trips the live pages read), `run_eod_shadow_score.py` (writes the `shadow_exit_results.jsonl` that `/shadow-results` displays).
- **`AlphaQuant_LLM_MarketView`** (09:15) and **`AlphaQuant_LLM_InPlayReview`** (09:40) write the JSON snapshots that `/daily-view` reads.

## At-risk-of-stale pages — what an EOD update+validate step must refresh/verify

These are the surfaces that do **not** self-recompute fully on load and depend on an upstream task having run:

1. **`/daily-review-v2` LLM narrative** — cached JSON (`daily_narratives/{day}.json`). Stale/absent if the 16:10 Daily Review task didn't run. *Verify: today's narrative file exists with today's timestamp; else hit `?regenerate=1`.*
2. **`/daily-view` (9:15 / 9:40 LLM reports)** — pure snapshots; show "not generated yet" if the LLM tasks failed. *Verify both `generated_at` stamps are today.*
3. **`/shadow-results`** — displays `shadow_exit_results.jsonl` with no recompute; stale if `run_eod_shadow_score.py` (16:50) failed. *Verify today's rows present.*
4. **`/trade-review` (legacy)** — serves a cache snapshot; relies on its own `stale_warning`. *Trust/verify the staleness banner; rebuild with `?refresh=1` if flagged.*
5. **`/morning-decision-board`** — cached by default; needs `?refresh=1` for current.

Everything else (**/truth, /autopsy, /what-if-risk, /decision-quality, /system-validation, /system-timeline, /edge-tunes, /planning, /current-strategy**) recomputes live from `broker_orders_unified.csv` / `eod_debrief` / state-file mtimes, so it is always current the moment the page loads — the dependency there is only that `eod_debrief.py` / `eod_reconciliation.py` (16:50) and the bot's broker-truth CSV are up to date.

**One structural note:** the only freshness guard that compares saved-vs-current source mtimes is in the legacy `/trade-review` cache path. The live `/daily-review-v2` has no "narrative is stale relative to today's trades" warning — if the 16:10 task fails, the page silently shows yesterday's (or no) narrative beside today's live trades. Sharp question, and **no — I don't agree, and you're right to push on it.** Here's the honest engineering truth: **no test can prove the absence of bugs** (you can only prove their *presence*). And this particular audit is the *wrong tool* for "run after every change," for three concrete reasons:

## No, I don't agree — and here's the honest version
**No test can prove a system is bug-free.** You can only ever prove a bug *exists*, never that none do. So that audit can't "assure failure-free." And as a *run-after-every-change* tool it was the wrong shape anyway: it's a manual, interpretive prompt (a human/agent could skip a step or mark PASS wrongly), it's point-in-time, and it predated everything we built today.

## So I built the right thing instead — an automated gate
**`audit_does_it_work.py`** — one command, deterministic, ~1 minute, single PASS/FAIL. Run it after any change or serious coding. It aggregates everything we've been building all week into one verdict:

| | Check | What it proves |
|---|---|---|
| A | regression suite (REG-01..27) | no known bug-class regressed |
| B | reliability drill | every fault detector still fires (no deaf alarm) |
| C | dashboard validate | pages tie to broker truth, caches fresh |
| D | preflight | live processes up + survivable |
| E | ORB preflight | entry-path gates green |

**It proved itself on the first run.** It came back **FAIL** — and correctly caught a real verify-load issue: I'd edited `orb_runner`/`risk_config` today but `run_bot` had been up since 7:14 AM, so its StartTime predated the edits (rule #13). I restarted the bot (clean supervisor respawn, market closed, flat — PID 388, 7:22 PM), re-ran, and it went **PASS 5/5**. That FAIL→fix→PASS loop is exactly the behavior you want before calling a change "shipped."

## What "PASS" honestly means
**Not** "bug-free forever." It means: *no known failure-mode regressed, and every alarm still works.* When we hit a **new** bug, we add a lock for it (a regression test or drill case), and from then on the gate catches it. That's how the assurance compounds — each bug we've ever seen can never silently return.

I also relabeled the old prompt so they're not confused: **the gate runs after every change; the prompt is the occasional deep adversarial hunt** for the *next* unknown bug class (which then becomes a new lock in the gate).

So: run `audit_does_it_work.py` before you trust any change. It's green right now, with today's work (9:35 gate, $500 cap, B1, dashboard, HTB/restricted) fully loaded and verified.

## First, untangle "the gate" — it's been two different things
This is the source of the confusion:
1. **The in-play *filter* (`ORB_INPLAY_GATE`)** — a selection filter that scored 9:35 candidates on RelVol / move-size / "exhaustion." **This** is the one that worked *backwards* — it rejected the quiet names that actually won and kept the ones that lost. It's been **OFF since 6/28**.
2. **The 9:35 *entry* gate (`ORB_935_ENTRIES_ENABLED=False`)** — what I flipped on 6/30. It doesn't filter; it **turns off 9:35 entries entirely.**

**So, are we trading at 9:35 now? No.** The 9:30–9:35 scanner still *runs* (it computes the opening range, ranks candidates, and logs them so we keep measuring), but it **submits zero orders.** Today: 0 from 9:35, all 25 from re-arm.

## Why the 9:35 system is "so wrong" — and where I was wrong
The 9:35 logic is an **opening-range breakout**: take the first 5 minutes' high/low, then buy a break above / short a break below, betting it continues. I'd told you the loss was mostly "chasing extended/spent gaps." **The data doesn't really support that.** Look at the 9:35 losers by how extended they were at entry:

| Move at entry | trades | net | per-trade | win% |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **<4% (low-conviction)** | 37 | **−$3,279** | **−$89** | 51% |
| 4–7% | 19 | −$270 | −$14 | 58% |
| >7% (extended) | 9 | −$4 | ~$0 | 67% |

Winners and losers had basically the **same** extension (~4%). The bleed is **broad — and actually worst on the *low-conviction* names**, not the big gappers. The extended ones roughly broke even (strong momentum offsets the occasional MU-style blowup).

So the real "why" isn't "we chase tops." It's simpler and worse: **the opening 5-minute range is just a bad signal.** The first five minutes is the noisiest, most-random part of the day — the opening auction imbalance, overnight digestion, max whipsaw. A range built in that chaos doesn't predict continuation, so its breakouts fail across the board. We built a system that makes a *decision* off the market's most *undecided* five minutes. That's the flaw.

## Why re-arm is better
Same breakout *structure*, different *context*. Re-arm scans at 10:35+, after the opening noise has burned off. A name breaking out then has usually built an hour of real price action — a genuine base — so the break is more likely a real trend, not an opening head-fake. **The edge isn't the logic, it's the timing:** waiting for the market to actually make up its mind.

## Should we park the 9:35 gate and run re-arm all day from 9:30?
- **Park 9:35: yes — keep it off.** The data is unambiguous (−$30/trade vs re-arm's +$1.2). The scanner keeps logging so we can re-visit if a real signal appears.
- **Run re-arm from 9:30: don't assume it — *test* it first.** This is the exact trap to avoid: if re-arm wins *because it waits for settling*, then running it at 9:35 just re-imports the opening-noise losses under a different name. We have **zero** re-arm data from 9:30–10:35 (it doesn't run then), so I can't answer it from the numbers — and guessing is how we got the backwards filter in the first place. The right move is a **shadow test**: add an early re-arm scan (9:35, 10:00) that only *logs* what it would do, score it for a week or two, and let the data decide. If the early window wins → turn it on and capture that dead 9:30–10:35 hour. If it loses → the edge is the timing, and we leave the gap.

**One honest caveat over all of this:** re-arm is only ~*breakeven* (+$1.2/trade, slightly negative post-6/19). So extending its hours doesn't create an edge — it just spreads a flat strategy across more of the day. Stopping the 9:35 bleed was the big, clean win; the *next* real dollars are in edge quality (the EOD-flatten bleeders, and whether re-arm has a true edge at all).

<result>Based on the official Claude Code documentation, here are the authoritative answers to your questions:

## Summary

**1. Built-in feature to access the same running local CLI session from a different device?**

**No native feature for this.** Claude Code does not have a "follow my session" mechanism. A session running in a terminal on machine A is not directly viewable or controllable from device B.

**2. "Remote control" / "remote access" / "share session" toggle?**

**Yes, but it's different than you might expect.** Claude Code has **Remote Control**, but it is not a setting — it's a feature activated by running commands:
- `claude remote-control` (server mode on the VPS)
- `claude --remote-control` (interactive session with remote access)
- `/remote-control` (enable remote on an existing session)

**3. Cloud sync to claude.ai or mobile app?**

**Partially, via Remote Control.** When you activate Remote Control, the session does NOT move to the cloud. Instead:
- The local session stays running on your VPS
- Anthropic routes remote connections (from claude.ai/code, or the Claude iOS/Android mobile apps) back to that local VPS process
- The web and mobile interfaces are a **window into your local session** — your files, MCP servers, and tools all stay available
- **The VPS process must stay running.** If you close the terminal, quit the process, or the machine goes offline for &gt;10 minutes, the session ends

**4. The `claude --resume` feature?**

**Local-only.** `--resume` resumes a session from local transcript files stored in `~/.claude/projects/&lt;project&gt;/&lt;session-id&gt;.jsonl`. It does **not** pull sessions from the cloud or work across machines. To use it on a different machine, you would need to manually copy the transcript files — there is no built-in cross-machine resume.

**5. "Claude Code on the web" or remote-agent capability?**

**Yes, but separate from your running session.** Claude Code on the web runs in Anthropic-managed cloud infrastructure, completely independent of your local VPS session. It would NOT give you access to your VPS session; it is a separate cloud session with no access to your local files or MCP servers.

## The Key Distinction

**To access your running VPS session from a phone or another laptop:**

Use **Remote Control** (`claude remote-control` on the VPS). This keeps your session on the VPS and streams it to remote devices via the Anthropic API.

**NOT** a built-in feature that makes a local CLI session portable or cloudable. The session runs locally; the interface is remote.

**Docs reference:**
- Remote Control: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/remote-control.md
- Sessions: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sessions.md
- How Claude Code works (execution environments): https://code.claude.com/docs/en/how-claude-code-works.md</result>

That bad entry hit a latent logic bug: `holiday_reason()` returns a truthy value for early-close days *and* full holidays alike, and `orb_multiscan`/`orb_runner` skip **all** trading on any truthy `holiday_reason`. So the bot treated a normal open trading day as a full closure and **armed zero entries all day** — proven by dry-run: `run_multiscan(...)` → `{'status':'holiday','detail':'EARLY_CLOSE: Day before Independence Day'}`.

Great question — and honestly it cuts right to the hardest part of the whole shadow concept. Let me verify what's actually running before I explain (I don't want to hand-wave this), then give you a clear mental model.
Verified — and your instinct in that last question is exactly right. Here's the real picture.

## What "the shadow" actually is
The shadow is **not a running bot.** Nothing in it places orders, and nothing in it touches the live bot or the market. It's a set of **read-only "what if?" scripts** that ask: *"Given data we already logged, what WOULD have happened if we'd done X differently?"*

Think of it as a **flight simulator running on yesterday's weather**, versus the live bot which is the actual plane in the air. The simulator can't crash the plane — it just replays history with a tweak.

## How many "things"?
About **30 analysis tools** exist in `strategy-research/` (plus 2 exit-replay harnesses in the bot). But they're **on-demand, not all running at once** — I fire one up when we're studying a specific idea (like `l1_unconfirmed_leash` for the 30-min time-stop you approved). Only **2** are on any schedule. So it's a *toolbox of ~30 studies*, with usually 0–1 active at a time — not a fleet constantly running.

## Do we apply it to our trades, or the whole market? — This is the key split
It depends on whether it's an **exit** test or an **entry** test, and they are fundamentally different:

**Exit shadows** (most of them — the time-stop, the $500 cap, the chandelier): applied to the **real trades we actually took.** We have the real entry and we logged the price path afterward. The shadow just replays a *different exit rule* on that *same real trade* → "what P&L would this exit have gotten on the exact trade we really did?" **High fidelity**, because the entry and the price path are real and fixed — only the exit decision changes.

**Entry shadows** (what you asked about): applied to the **whole market's candidates**, because a different entry rule would take *different trades* — ones that **never actually happened.**

## Your killer question — and you nailed it
> *"If the shadow changed how we ENTER, how could it pick up on the change if it wasn't trading like a bot?"*

**It can't — not the way an exit shadow can. And the system openly admits it.** That's literally why there are three trust levels baked into the code:

| Tier | What it is | Trust |
|---|---|---|
| `broker_truth` | what actually happened | highest |
| `replay` | a different **exit** replayed on **real** trades | medium |
| `one_minute_counterfactual_low` | **simulated** trades that never happened (an entry change) | **LOW — never a verdict** |

An entry shadow lands in that bottom tier because it has to *guess* the things only real trading answers:
- Would we actually have **gotten filled** at that price? (real fills slip)
- What happened **between** the 1-minute bars? (a 1-min bar can't tell you if the stop or the target hit first inside that minute)
- Would taking that trade have **used a slot** that changed the other trades?

So an entry shadow gives a **directional hint** ("this filter looks like it'd help"), never proof.

## So what do we actually do for entry changes?
We let the **live market be the judge.** Instead of trusting an entry shadow, we deploy the entry change **live but tagged**, and compare real broker P&L. That's exactly what we did with the 9:35 path: we gated it OFF live and let the re-arm path run, then compared *real* fills — because, as you said, a shadow can't fake real trading.

**One-line summary:** exit ideas we can prove in the shadow; entry ideas the shadow can only *hint* at — they need a real, tagged live test to trust. Your confusion was actually the correct instinct.

## Yes, it's possible. But there are two very different versions — pick carefully.

**Version A — a backtester / research sim** (replay historical data → run the bot's signal logic → model fills → log trades + P&L). **This is the high-value one.** It's exactly what solves the problem from our shadow conversation: it's the only clean way to test **entry** changes without burning live SIM days.

**Version B — a live paper-sim that *replaces* TradeStation SIM** (bot trades live market data through our own engine). **Low value — don't build this.** TS SIM already gives us realistic fills + real data *for free*. Rebuilding it ourselves means reinventing the wheel with **worse** fill realism and more maintenance. It buys us almost nothing.

So the real question is "should we build the backtester?" — and my answer is yes, with eyes open.

## The catch (it's the same one from the shadow talk)
A home sim **models** fills — it can't perfectly reproduce real ones (slippage, partial fills, whether your stop or target hit first inside a 1-minute bar). That's the identical low-fidelity problem shadows have. **The danger is false confidence:** an optimistic fill model makes a losing strategy look profitable. This project has been burned by exactly that before (an old backtest showed −99.92%).

**But we have a real edge that most backtests don't:** we log every *real* TS fill. So we can (a) **calibrate** the fill model's slippage against what actually happened, and (b) **prove** the sim is trustworthy by making it **reproduce a known real day** before we believe a single number it produces. That acceptance gate is already written into the plan. Without that validation, a home sim is just a fancier low-fidelity shadow.

## How much work
Not from zero — it's *assembly + hardening*, not a new build:
- **MVP** (replay a handful of historical days, run the real ORB signal logic, calibrated fill model, P&L ledger, reproduce one known day): a few focused build sessions.
- **The expensive part** is running the **real bot code** against the sim rather than a fork (the live modules call `TSClient()` directly — making that cleanly swappable for a mock is the actual engineering), plus fidelity hardening. Human-dev-equivalent that's weeks; I ship faster, but budget real iteration for the fidelity work.

## The bill (dollars)
Small. **1-minute bars come from the TS API we already pay for → ~$0.** The only optional cost is a tick-data vendor (Polygon/Databento, ~$50–200/mo) *if* we ever need sub-minute fill precision. Compute runs on the VPS (negligible). No extra broker account. **The real "cost" is my build/iteration time, not money.**

## My recommendation
Build **Version A as a funnel, not a verdict:**
1. It screens many ideas fast + cheap (especially **entry** changes, which we can't shadow and don't want to burn live SIM days on).
2. **Validate fidelity first** — it must reproduce a known real result before we trust it.
3. Survivors still go to **live tagged SIM** for the real proof. The sim doesn't *replace* live SIM — it makes live SIM time far more productive by pre-filtering the junk.

It's gated (`PROP-LEARN`), so it'd go through a proposal + your approval, and that reproduce-a-known-day acceptance criterion is what keeps us from trusting a broken sim.

**Bottom line:** worth building, cheap in dollars, real in effort — but its entire value hinges on validating it against real fills first. Want me to write up the concrete build plan (MVP scope + the fidelity-validation gate) as a proposal for you to look at?

## Why your version actually is valuable
Three real reasons, and they're not small:

1. **It's a forward test — so it can't overfit.** This is the big one. The historical backtester (Version A) replays the *past*, which you can accidentally curve-fit to. Your live shadow tests a change on **unseen, real-time data going forward** — the gold standard for trusting a result. That's a genuine advantage over the backtester, not a lateral move.

2. **It doesn't pollute the SIM account.** Right now, to test an exit change I have to deploy it to the one live SIM bot — which changes that bot and contaminates its P&L, its clean-day counter, its stats. Your shadow lets the SIM account stay clean while you experiment.

3. **True parallel A/B.** One SIM account can only run one version at a time. Your shadow lets "current exit" and "new exit" run **side-by-side on the exact same live tape** — apples to apples, same day, same fills-ish. You literally can't do that on a single SIM account.

And a bonus: **it's the same engine as the backtester.** Version A = feed the engine historical data. Version B = feed the same engine the live quote stream and run the modified strategy. Building A gets you ~80% of B. They're not either/or.

## The one honest caveat (smaller than I made it sound)
It still *models* fills rather than getting real ones — but on **live** data, for our **marketable-limit** order style, a fill model calibrated against our logged real TS fills is actually pretty good. So the ladder becomes: **backtest (fast, overfit-risk) → your live shadow (forward, clean, parallel) → TS SIM (real fills) → live money.** Your shadow fills the missing "forward test with no consequences" rung. Good instinct.

## One alternative worth knowing before we build anything
There may be a shortcut to *most* of what you want, with **real** fills and almost no build: **a second TS SIM account.** TS hands out SIM accounts; we already have two (equity + the futures one for H5). Point a second bot instance running the *modified* strategy at a **third** SIM account, and you get:
- **Real TS fills** (no fill-modeling problem at all — highest fidelity)
- Parallel, forward, live A/B against the main bot
- Zero pollution of the primary SIM
- Almost no code — it's the same bot, different account + a config flag

**Trade-off:** a second SIM account gives you *one* variant with real fills; our home shadow (B) gives you *unlimited* variants with modeled fills, full control, and doubles as the backtester.

## My honest recommendation
- If you want a **live parallel shadow soon, with the best fills, least work** → **second TS SIM account.** That's likely the fastest, highest-fidelity path to exactly the "test-then-promote" flow you described.
- If you want a **research platform** that runs many variants, tests entries at scale, replays history, and isn't dependent on TS → **build the engine (A+B).** More work, modeled fills, but far more powerful long-term.

They're complementary — and honestly, doing the second-SIM-account first (cheap, real fills) while we build the engine in parallel is probably the smartest sequence.

## The line: remove BUGS, never remove LOSSES

Your instinct to clean the data is right — **and exit-backtesting on our real trades is the *high-fidelity* kind** (real entries, real price paths, just swap the exit). Good call. But there's one razor line we can't cross, and the table shows exactly why.

**6/25 (MU) and 6/29 (COHR) are the "problem days" you're describing — but those were NOT bugs.** The bot entered MU and COHR *per its rules*, and they moved against us. They're **real losses the strategy produced.** And here's the kicker:

> **Those two days are the exact data that gave us our two best exit fixes.** The $500 dollar-cap was discovered *because* of 6/29 (it recovered +$1,672 that day). The 30-min time-stop was discovered *because* of MU on 6/25 (turned −$1,670 into −$50). **If we'd deleted those days, we'd have found neither.**

That's the trap: an exit strategy's entire *job* is to handle the trades that go against you. If you remove the losers before testing, you're testing exits **only on winners** — the backtest comes back "this is great!" and then loses real money live. **This project already got burned by exactly this** (an old backtest showed −99.92%). Deleting inconvenient losses is the #1 way a backtest lies to you.

## What SHOULD be removed (the real cleaning)
Not losses — **bugs.** Trades where a *code defect* made the bot do something it wasn't designed to do:
- **Pre-5/26** trades (different strategy config — already excluded by baseline).
- **Bug-driven trades** — the HTB-filter-broken periods (traded names it never should have), the calendar-outage days (didn't trade), any day a filter was broken. Those aren't "the strategy," they're a defect.

Key subtlety: this is **per-trade tagging, not per-day deletion.** Example — 6/30 had a broken HTB path on the 9:35 side, but the re-arm still took *legit* trades that day. You keep the legit ones, drop the bug ones.

## One honest flag
I scanned the post-6/08 broker record and **I don't actually see an "only-HTB-stocks day"** in it — the HTB issues shrank the 9:35 book, but the re-arm path still traded normal names. So before we exclude any "problem period," we verify it against the documented incident log (SESSION_LOG / bot_alerts) rather than deleting by feel. That verification *is* the cleaning work.

## The build
A **"clean cohort" tagger**: read `broker_orders_unified.csv`, tag every trade as `legit` or `bug-driven (+reason)` using our documented incident history, **keep all legit trades — winners and losers, MU included** — and exclude only the true bug-trades. Then backtest exits on that clean-but-honest set.

**Bottom line: we clean out the *bugs*, we keep the *losers*.** The losers aren't noise — they're the signal. Want me to build the clean-cohort tagger and show you exactly which trades get flagged bug vs kept (with the reason for each), so you can see nothing legit is being scrubbed?

The design is back. The headline finding is important: **every existing replayer handles exits against real entries — nothing re-runs entry logic offline**, which shapes the whole build. Let me pull the actual blueprint (architecture, MVP, fill model, effort, risks) cleanly:
The blueprint is excellent — and it's mostly **reuse** (we already built ~80% of this in prior shadow work). Here's the honest distillation, one surprise that changes the plan, and the recommendation.

## The design (two phases, not one)
- **Phase 1 — the exit backtester (MVP, ~4–6h, ~80% reuse):** `shadow_exit_harness.replay()` already replays alternate exits on our real trades and anchors to broker truth. The only genuinely new pieces are a **calibrated fill model** (from our 719 real fills) and a **fidelity gate**. This is buildable now.
- **Phase 2 — the forward live-shadow (your "shadow SIM," ~1–2 weeks):** the real net-new build — an offline **entry engine**, a sim clock, and an order-matching `SimClient`. Bigger, and it should wait.

## The surprise that changes the plan (honest)
**We only have dense price-path data for ~6 days (6/18–6/26).** Polling collapsed after that (6/30 = 2 polls, 7/01 = 6). So the *trustworthy* exit-backtest set is those ~6 dense days — **not all 217 trades.** Two consequences:
1. We tune on a small window → real overfitting risk (I'll run leave-one-out + MU-in/out robustness, and bring a proposal, never tune inline).
2. **We should fix the price-path logging going forward** so future backtests have far more data. That's a cheap, high-value change.

## The anti-lie guardrail (built into the plan)
The fidelity gate **must reproduce MU −$1,670 and COHR −$1,975** before any tuned number counts. *If the fill model can't reproduce the losers, the model is wrong — not the losers.* Plus a planted-mismatch self-test. This is the direct guard against the −99.92% trap.

## The one risk I want to name loudly
Our fills are **SIM fills**, which are typically *more generous* than live. The model can only honestly claim **SIM-fidelity** — and a forward shadow built on it **launders that optimism forward in real time.** So: **build and validate the exit backtester first; do NOT build the forward shadow until the fill model proves out.** That's the blueprint's recommendation and I agree with it.

## My recommendation on sequencing
1. **Build Phase 1 (exit backtester) now** — calibrate fills → fill model → fidelity gate (reproduce MU/COHR) → backtest the clean cohort's dense days.
2. **Hold Phase 2 (forward shadow)** until the fill model is validated.
3. **Separately, fix price-path logging** so we stop starving future backtests.

**What this reveals:** our **entries are tight** (the 5-bps collar is working — nothing slips past it), and **marketable-limit exits fill at the touch (~0 slip)**. The *only* place slippage genuinely bites is the **stop-market exits** — the tail runs to +19–41 bps, which is exactly where losers get worse than the nominal stop — **but we only have 14–18 of them, so that estimate has wide error bars.** That thin sample is the single biggest fidelity caveat, and I've flagged it in the model so we don't over-trust it.

The root cause is more nuanced than the headline — and important. Let me pull the synthesis (ranked fixes, deploy plan) cleanly:
The investigation is done, and the honest answer is more useful than the headline. Here it is straight.

## Are we using the TW efficiently? No — but not for the reason it looked like.

The "92% gaps / 46s" number was **mostly a measurement artifact**, not a broken stream. The real story is sharper:

**The TW is reading the wrong price.** It feeds its exit decision off the **last *trade* price** only (`q.get("Last")`), and TradeStation's SIM quote feed is *coalesced* — it pushes a quote only when a field changes, and on quiet mid-caps that's every 15–30 seconds between trades (the AAPL smoke test got **1 quote in 10.3 seconds**). So between trade prints, the **bid/ask are moving continuously but the TW is blind to them** — it can't see the chandelier level get crossed until the next trade prints. That's why it's currently **roughly a duplicate of the 30-second poller, with extra deploy risk.** On 7/02 it actually *lost* — `exit_bot_v2` beat it on 8 of 9 exits.

**Critical reassurance: there is NO safety hole.** This is a *precision* problem, not a *coverage* one. Every position is always covered by the 22-second poll + the 30-min time-stop + the always-on 1.4×ATR broker resting stop, and the ownership lease fails *open*. "TW blind for 22s" never means "nobody's watching."

## The fix that actually makes it tick-by-tick
**Feed the decision off the mid (bid+ask)/2 when the last trade is stale.** The mid updates continuously, so the TW would finally see the level cross in real time — the tick-level edge it's *supposed* to have. Plus three cleanups (fix the misleading gap metric, reset the reconnect-gap bug, move REST calls off the read thread). **Bonus:** that same reliable stream gives us a dense quote-level price path for the backtester — better than the 1-minute logger I built.

# PDF Processing Guide

## Overview

This guide covers essential PDF processing operations using Python libraries and command-line tools. For advanced features, JavaScript libraries, and detailed examples, see REFERENCE.md. If you need to fill out a PDF form, read FORMS.md and follow its instructions.

## Quick Start

```python
from pypdf import PdfReader, PdfWriter

# Read a PDF
reader = PdfReader("document.pdf")
print(f"Pages: {len(reader.pages)}")

# Extract text
text = ""
for page in reader.pages:
    text += page.extract_text()
```

## Python Libraries

### pypdf - Basic Operations

#### Merge PDFs
```python
from pypdf import PdfWriter, PdfReader

writer = PdfWriter()
for pdf_file in ["doc1.pdf", "doc2.pdf", "doc3.pdf"]:
    reader = PdfReader(pdf_file)
    for page in reader.pages:
        writer.add_page(page)

with open("merged.pdf", "wb") as output:
    writer.write(output)
```

#### Split PDF
```python
reader = PdfReader("input.pdf")
for i, page in enumerate(reader.pages):
    writer = PdfWriter()
    writer.add_page(page)
    with open(f"page_{i+1}.pdf", "wb") as output:
        writer.write(output)
```

#### Extract Metadata
```python
reader = PdfReader("document.pdf")
meta = reader.metadata
print(f"Title: {meta.title}")
print(f"Author: {meta.author}")
print(f"Subject: {meta.subject}")
print(f"Creator: {meta.creator}")
```

#### Rotate Pages
```python
reader = PdfReader("input.pdf")
writer = PdfWriter()

page = reader.pages[0]
page.rotate(90)  # Rotate 90 degrees clockwise
writer.add_page(page)

with open("rotated.pdf", "wb") as output:
    writer.write(output)
```

### pdfplumber - Text and Table Extraction

#### Extract Text with Layout
```python
import pdfplumber

with pdfplumber.open("document.pdf") as pdf:
    for page in pdf.pages:
        text = page.extract_text()
        print(text)
```

#### Extract Tables
```python
with pdfplumber.open("document.pdf") as pdf:
    for i, page in enumerate(pdf.pages):
        tables = page.extract_tables()
        for j, table in enumerate(tables):
            print(f"Table {j+1} on page {i+1}:")
            for row in table:
                print(row)
```

#### Advanced Table Extraction
```python
import pandas as pd

with pdfplumber.open("document.pdf") as pdf:
    all_tables = []
    for page in pdf.pages:
        tables = page.extract_tables()
        for table in tables:
            if table:  # Check if table is not empty
                df = pd.DataFrame(table[1:], columns=table[0])
                all_tables.append(df)

# Combine all tables
if all_tables:
    combined_df = pd.concat(all_tables, ignore_index=True)
    combined_df.to_excel("extracted_tables.xlsx", index=False)
```

### reportlab - Create PDFs

#### Basic PDF Creation
```python
from reportlab.lib.pagesizes import letter
from reportlab.pdfgen import canvas

c = canvas.Canvas("hello.pdf", pagesize=letter)
width, height = letter

# Add text
c.drawString(100, height - 100, "Hello World!")
c.drawString(100, height - 120, "This is a PDF created with reportlab")

# Add a line
c.line(100, height - 140, 400, height - 140)

# Save
c.save()
```

#### Create PDF with Multiple Pages
```python
from reportlab.lib.pagesizes import letter
from reportlab.platypus import SimpleDocTemplate, Paragraph, Spacer, PageBreak
from reportlab.lib.styles import getSampleStyleSheet

doc = SimpleDocTemplate("report.pdf", pagesize=letter)
styles = getSampleStyleSheet()
story = []

# Add content
title = Paragraph("Report Title", styles['Title'])
story.append(title)
story.append(Spacer(1, 12))

body = Paragraph("This is the body of the report. " * 20, styles['Normal'])
story.append(body)
story.append(PageBreak())

# Page 2
story.append(Paragraph("Page 2", styles['Heading1']))
story.append(Paragraph("Content for page 2", styles['Normal']))

# Build PDF
doc.build(story)
```

#### Subscripts and Superscripts

**IMPORTANT**: Never use Unicode subscript/superscript characters (₀₁₂₃₄₅₆₇₈₉, ⁰¹²³⁴⁵⁶⁷⁸⁹) in ReportLab PDFs. The built-in fonts do not include these glyphs, causing them to render as solid black boxes.

Instead, use ReportLab's XML markup tags in Paragraph objects:
```python
from reportlab.platypus import Paragraph
from reportlab.lib.styles import getSampleStyleSheet

styles = getSampleStyleSheet()

# Subscripts: use <sub> tag
chemical = Paragraph("H<sub>2</sub>O", styles['Normal'])

# Superscripts: use <super> tag
squared = Paragraph("x<super>2</super> + y<super>2</super>", styles['Normal'])
```

For canvas-drawn text (not Paragraph objects), manually adjust font the size and position rather than using Unicode subscripts/superscripts.

## Command-Line Tools

### pdftotext (poppler-utils)
```bash
# Extract text
pdftotext input.pdf output.txt

# Extract text preserving layout
pdftotext -layout input.pdf output.txt

# Extract specific pages
pdftotext -f 1 -l 5 input.pdf output.txt  # Pages 1-5
```

### qpdf
```bash
# Merge PDFs
qpdf --empty --pages file1.pdf file2.pdf -- merged.pdf

# Split pages
qpdf input.pdf --pages . 1-5 -- pages1-5.pdf
qpdf input.pdf --pages . 6-10 -- pages6-10.pdf

# Rotate pages
qpdf input.pdf output.pdf --rotate=+90:1  # Rotate page 1 by 90 degrees

# Remove password
qpdf --password: [REDACTED] --decrypt encrypted.pdf decrypted.pdf
```

### pdftk (if available)
```bash
# Merge
pdftk file1.pdf file2.pdf cat output merged.pdf

# Split
pdftk input.pdf burst

# Rotate
pdftk input.pdf rotate 1east output rotated.pdf
```

## Common Tasks

### Extract Text from Scanned PDFs
```python
# Requires: pip install pytesseract pdf2image
import pytesseract
from pdf2image import convert_from_path

# Convert PDF to images
images = convert_from_path('scanned.pdf')

# OCR each page
text = ""
for i, image in enumerate(images):
    text += f"Page {i+1}:\n"
    text += pytesseract.image_to_string(image)
    text += "\n\n"

print(text)
```

### Add Watermark
```python
from pypdf import PdfReader, PdfWriter

# Create watermark (or load existing)
watermark = PdfReader("watermark.pdf").pages[0]

# Apply to all pages
reader = PdfReader("document.pdf")
writer = PdfWriter()

for page in reader.pages:
    page.merge_page(watermark)
    writer.add_page(page)

with open("watermarked.pdf", "wb") as output:
    writer.write(output)
```

### Extract Images
```bash
# Using pdfimages (poppler-utils)
pdfimages -j input.pdf output_prefix

# This extracts all images as output_prefix-000.jpg, output_prefix-001.jpg, etc.
```

### Password Protection
```python
from pypdf import PdfReader, PdfWriter

reader = PdfReader("input.pdf")
writer = PdfWriter()

for page in reader.pages:
    writer.add_page(page)

# Add password
writer.encrypt("userpassword", "ownerpassword")

with open("encrypted.pdf", "wb") as output:
    writer.write(output)
```

## The design — one new supervised daemon

**Flow:** warning fires → notifier mirrors it to the queue → a small always-on daemon (`warning_responder.py`, watching the queue near-real-time) picks up the new FAIL/CRIT → fires a **headless Claude review** (`claude -p`) that (1) verifies it against live truth, (2) works out *what happened + the fix*, (3) sends **you** a Telegram message like:

> ⚠️ *CSHV: rel_trading_is_thinking FAIL* — **What happened:** run_bot's loop stalled >4 min at 9:30, self-recovered (one-off). **Fix:** none needed; watching for recurrence.

→ then marks it triaged so you never get the same raw alert twice without context.

**Built-in:** triggers on FAIL/CRIT only (not INFO — avoids the H5-spam class), dedup + a cooldown so a flapping warning can't spam reviews (bounds token cost), ~20–60s latency, supervised by `supervisor_guardian` (24/5).

## Two honest constraints
1. It has to be a **separate headless mechanism** — *this* chat only runs when you message me or the 15-min cron fires. The daemon + `claude -p` is what makes it real-time. You and I both still get the raw alert; the daemon adds the analysis on top.
2. Each review **spends tokens** (dedup keeps it to a few/day normally). And it's one-shot analysis — great for "what happened / here's the fix," not deep multi-step debugging (that still comes to you or me).

Also, let's run a test on our last day of trading. That was a negative day. I wanna know how many of the trades were confirmed and unconfirmed and how many losers and winners in each category.

**Claude Code:**

This is a focused 2×2 on 7/02 — I'll compute it directly from broker truth (the news workflow keeps running in the background). "Confirmed vs unconfirmed" maps cleanly to the exit reason: a trade time-stopped at 30 min = never confirmed; a candle-close exit = confirmed. Let me build the grid:
Here's the 2×2 for **7/02** (last trading day, −$770, 20 round-trips), from broker truth. "Confirmed" = the trade's favorable move actually reached the +0.15×ATR confirm threshold (so it rode the candle-close exit); "unconfirmed" = it never did and got flushed by the 30-min time-stop.

| | Winners | Losers | Total |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| **Confirmed** | **1** (+$83) | **0** | 1 (+$83) |
| **Unconfirmed** | **4** (+$133) | **15** (−$986) | 19 (−$853) |
| **Total** | 5 | 15 | 20 |

- **Confirmed: 1 trade — and it won** (MCD +$83). It was the *only* trade all day that showed real follow-through in our favor.
- **Unconfirmed: 19 trades** — the 4 "winners" were tiny (+$133 total, avg +$33; SNDK/STX/DELL/ADBE just happened to be slightly green when the 30-min stop fired) and **all 15 losers were unconfirmed.**

## What this actually tells us
The striking part: **confirmation was near-perfectly predictive.** Every single loser failed to confirm, and the one trade that confirmed won. The entire day's loss (−$853) lived in the unconfirmed bucket. In plain terms — on 7/02 the market gave us almost **no follow-through** (5% confirmation rate); we entered 20 breakouts and 19 just went nowhere.

**Two honest caveats before you read too much into it:**
1. **You can't filter on this at entry** — confirmation happens *after* you're in the trade. It's a read on the *day's* quality (choppy, no follow-through), not a knob we can turn pre-entry. It's exactly what the 30-min time-stop is designed to catch.
2. **7/02 was a compromised day** — the morning was lost to the outage, so we only traded the lower-quality afternoon re-arm tape, and it was the first live day of the time-stop. A clean full session (Monday) is a fairer test of the confirmation rate.

The bigger signal: if this 1-in-20 confirmation rate persists on *clean* days, that's a real entry-quality problem worth chasing. If Monday looks normal (~50–60% like the pre-time-stop days), 7/02 was just a bad, degraded tape. Worth watching Monday's confirmed/unconfirmed split closely.

While the full ranked menu compiles, let me answer the specific thing you asked — because the 52-week high behavior is genuinely counterintuitive and it's a perfect entry point.

## What a stock does at its 52-week high / low

**Breaking to a NEW 52-week HIGH → it tends to keep going UP.** This surprises people (it *feels* like "it's too high, it'll pull back"), but it's one of the most durable, academically-documented effects in markets (the "52-week-high momentum" anomaly). Three reasons:
1. **No overhead supply.** Below a 52-week high, there are always people who bought higher and are waiting to "get out even" — that selling caps rallies. At a *new* high, *nobody is underwater.* There's no one waiting to sell. The path of least resistance is up.
2. **It's a demand signal** — something (earnings, a catalyst, institutional accumulation) is pushing it there.
3. **Anchoring bias** — traders anchor to the old high and under-react, so the move continues longer than it "should."

**Breaking a 52-week LOW → it tends to keep going DOWN** (capitulation, forced/margin selling, downside momentum) — which is a *short* setup, and it's exactly why 52-week lows are dangerous to buy ("catching a falling knife").

**The practical filter most pros actually use isn't the breakout itself — it's *proximity*:** a stock within a few percent of its 52-week high is "in a strong uptrend, buyers in control"; a stock stuck near its low has sellers in control. It's a **strength gauge you overlay on everything else.**

## How this maps to *us* (a day-trader, flat by close)
We don't hold for the multi-week move, so the 52-week high isn't our *trade* — it's **context that should bias our breakouts.** The obvious hypotheses to test:
- **Only take our long re-arm breakouts in names near/at their 52-week high** (strong names break clean) — and be cautious of long breakouts *into* an overhead 52-week high (sellers waiting = failure).
- The **intraday version of the same idea:** prior-day high, opening-range vs the 20-day range — a breakout that's *also* a multi-day high has no overhead supply.

## The broader landscape I'm digging into (the full menu is compiling)
The 52-week level is one of **seven families** of price-structure edge I've got researchers deep-diving right now, each mapped to our system + a way to test it with our data:
1. **Range extremes** (52-week / N-day highs & lows) ← the above
2. **Relative strength** (trade the strongest longs / weakest shorts vs the market & sector)
3. **Volume / float / short interest** (what really confirms a breakout; squeeze dynamics)
4. **Gaps & the open** (gap-and-go vs gap-fill — the most ORB-relevant of all)
5. **Key levels** (VWAP, prior-day H/L, round numbers, the 200-day moving average)
6. **Volatility & market regime** (breakouts work in calm trends, fail in choppy high-VIX tape — a "should we even trade today" gate)
7. **Time-of-day & momentum-vs-reversion** (which directly attacks our confirmation problem — *why* did only 1 of 20 confirm on 7/02)

When it lands I'll give you a **ranked menu** — the top ideas by (real edge) × (fits our intraday system) × (we can test it now with the data we have), plus the 2-3 I'd test *first* and a "don't bother" list so we don't chase dead ends. Back shortly with that.

# The two big edges (everything else is a variation)

## 🥇 #1 — Trade less on chop days (a market-regime gate). **HIGH**
This showed up **independently in three of the seven families** (volatility, time-of-day, key-levels) *and* it directly explains our worst day. On 7/02 only 1 of 20 confirmed and we lost −$770; on 7/01 the *same system* made +$1,183. The difference wasn't our entries — it was the **day**. Breakouts only work when the market is actually trending; on choppy, mean-reverting days they round-trip and die (exactly our "unconfirmed" bleed).
- **The idea:** classify each day (or each re-arm window) as TREND vs CHOP from SPY's own price action, and on chop days **cut deployment / reduce max positions / pause re-arms** — using the advisor control we already have.
- **Why it's the best:** it's a *risk knob on the whole book*, not a per-name alpha bet. It can't cut a winner (it just sizes down when the odds are bad). And the data's already logged.
- **This is the single highest-conviction idea from the entire deep dive.**

## 🥈 #2 — Stop entering *against* the day's trend (an alignment filter). **HIGH**
Four different families (relative strength, key-levels/VWAP, gaps, 52-week) all described the *same underlying thing* from different angles: **don't take a breakout that's fighting the tape.** Concretely, they're all proxies for "is this stock moving *with* strength today":
- **RS-alignment:** only go long if the stock is outperforming SPY (we already compute this — it's just not wired as a filter).
- **VWAP-side:** only go long above a rising VWAP (institutional fair value).
- **Overhead-supply veto:** skip long breakouts running straight into a prior 52-week/multi-day high (that's where breakouts stall and die — our stall-and-time-stop bleed).
- **Gap-with-trend:** breakouts whose gap agrees with the 5-day trend follow through better; giant "blow-off" gaps fill and fail.

**The catch (important):** these are largely the *same signal re-skinned* — they all correlate with "trending up today." So we **don't stack all four** — we test each, measure which one separates our winners from losers best, and add *the one*. Adding five correlated filters is how you overfit.

# Test these FIRST (cheap, testable now, low overfit risk)
1. **The chop-day study** — bucket our existing trades by SPY regime (trend vs chop) and read the expectancy per bucket. Pure measurement, zero live risk. If our losses cluster on chop days (I'd bet they do), the regime gate is validated. **Do this first.**
2. **The RS-alignment counterfactual** — we already log `rel_move_vs_spy`; split our trades by "aligned vs fighting the tape" and check the must-not-cut gate (does it kill losers without cutting winners?). One run.
3. **Per-window expectancy** — rank the six re-arm windows (9:45…14:35) by net result; the 12:35 lunch-lull window is the prime suspect for dead weight. Nearly free — the data's already tagged.

# Also promising (second tier)
- **Volume-scaled sizing** — size the position to the time-of-day liquidity, cutting slippage on thin late-day trades (a sizer, so must-not-cut-safe).
- **RelVol *persistence*** — prefer names with *sustained* volume over a one-print spike.

# Don't bother / dead ends (so we don't waste time)
- **"Capturing the 52-week-high premium"** — real, but it's a *weeks-to-months* portfolio effect. We're flat by 3:50 PM; we can't harvest it. We borrow it only as an intraday *filter*, never as a return source.
- **Float / short-interest / squeeze signals** — **data-blocked.** TradeStation doesn't expose float or short-interest, so we can't build these.
- **Day-of-week / seasonality** — real but tiny (a few basis points), swamped by our own trading costs.
- **New exit-path tweaks** — gated, and the $500 cap has beaten every exit rule we've tried.

# The honest caveat on all of it
Everything above is **hypothesis-grade** — our post-5/26 tape is thin, so any result needs N≥30 per bucket + out-of-sample validation before it touches the live path. These are ideas to *test*, not deploy. The good news: the machinery to test them (the trade-tape cohort, the AUC separation study, the net-of-cost fill model) already exists.

**My recommendation:** the chop-day regime study (#1) is the highest edge-per-effort thing we could do — it's read-only, uses data we have, and it targets the exact failure mode that cost us on 7/02. Want me to run that study now and show you whether our losses really do concentrate on choppy days?

## Edge hunt — the honest verdict (broker-truth tape, N=221, 6/18–7/02)

I ran real code against the real tape, three tests in parallel plus an adversarial synthesis. Baseline reproduced exactly: **221 round-trips, 131 win / 90 lose (59.3%), net −$3,371.**

**The blunt bottom line: no *entry* feature we log is a deployable edge at this N.** Best entry-knowable separator is AUC 0.398 — everything else (relvol, RS-vs-SPY, gap, move%, exhaustion) sits at 0.43–0.51, which is noise. Nothing near the 0.70 bar. But three things came out of this that matter:

**1. Our top hypothesis got *falsified* — and that's worth knowing.** The deep-dive's #1 idea ("losses concentrate on chop days") is **wrong in our data.** Day-level correlation between SPY choppiness and P&L is −0.16; the median split is *inverted* (higher-efficiency days lost more); the two big loss days (6/25, 6/29) were actually the *cleaner-trending* days. **Do not build a chop-day gate.** This is exactly why we test instead of trusting priors — I would have built that filter and it would have done nothing.

**2. The relvol lead is a head-fake — I'm explicitly telling you not to trade it.** Relative volume predicts *confirmation* well (day_relvol AUC 0.638, the best predictive hit in the study). But when I bucketed on **dollars**, the **low-relvol tertile is the only profitable one (+$1,004)**; high-relvol is −$1,629. Chasing relvol to chase confirmation *loses money*. It predicts the label and is anti-correlated with net-$. Seductive on the AUC number, dead on the P&L — killed.

**3. The one real, significant, robust signal is time-of-day** — but it lives in shadow, not the bot. Entry **before 11:00 ET wins 67.7%; after 11:00 wins 47.9%** — a 19.8pp gap, z=2.97 (significant), and it holds the same sign on **all 10 leave-one-day-out folds** (most robust thing in the tape). **The catch:** it does *not* convert to dollars yet — the early book actually loses slightly *more per trade*, and as a hard `BLOCK_ENTRIES_AFTER_TIME` it fails must-not-cut (cuts 45 real winners). Real win-rate edge, no money edge at this N.

**The most important finding: our edge is entirely in the EXIT, not the entry.** Confirmed trades (favorable move hits +0.15×ATR within 30 min) = **+$14,894 at 96.7% win**; unconfirmed = **−$14,156 at 9.1%**. That's not tradeable as an entry filter (confirm is known 30 min *after* entry) — but it *validates the exit stack we've been building*: the candle-close trail, the $500 cap, and the 30-min unconfirmed time-stop are aimed at exactly the cohort where all the losses live. **The money lever is the exit engine, and the parked confirmation-keyed-exit direction is where the real edge work is.**

One structural signal has a genuinely deployable *shape*: **"entry at/above the trailing-20-day high"** as a size-*down* gate — 2.1:1 loser-$-saved to winner-$-removed, and it's the one filter that would've caught our single biggest loser (MU 6/25, −$1,670). But MU alone drives 39% of what it saves — one trade — so it's suggestive, not proven.

- **B) 20d-high size-down gate** — deployable shape, catches the worst loser, but needs N to prove it's not just MU.

### 1. **What Must Be True on the VPS for the Phone to Be "Connected"**

The **Claude Code process on the VPS must be actively running and maintaining an outbound connection to Anthropic's API**. According to the [Remote Control documentation](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/remote-control):

&gt; "When you start Remote Control, it registers with the Anthropic API and polls for work. When you connect from another device, the server routes messages between the web or mobile client and your local session over a streaming connection."

**Key requirements:**
- The VPS-side `claude` process must be **actively running** (not backgrounded without polling)
- It maintains **outbound HTTPS-only** connections to `api.anthropic.com` (port 443)
- The session uses **short-lived, multi-purpose credentials** that expire independently
- The machine does **not** need to open inbound ports

**If the session was closed/restarted**, the VPS side stopped registering with the API, so the polling link broke. The phone still sees the old session in the list, but the connection status changes to "Disconnected" because the VPS process is no longer polling.

---

### 2. **How to Reconnect: Phone-Side vs. Machine-Side Actions**

**The reconnection requires a MACHINE-SIDE action.** According to the docs:

&gt; "If your laptop sleeps or your network drops, the session reconnects automatically when your machine comes back online."

and:

&gt; "Your local session keeps running without Remote Control. Run `/remote-control` to retry the connection, or start Claude Code without `--resume` to create a new Remote Control session."

**Phone-side actions do NOT reconnect:**
- Pull-to-refresh on the phone: does NOT work (the docs make no mention of this)
- Closing/reopening the session in the app: does NOT work if the VPS process isn't running
- Force-quitting the Claude app: does NOT help

**Machine-side actions that DO reconnect (in order of preference):**

1. **Re-run the Remote Control command on the VPS** (best option):
   ```bash
   claude remote-control
   ```
   Or, if the previous session is still in the system:
   ```bash
   claude remote-control --continue
   ```
   Or resume a specific session by ID:
   ```bash
   claude remote-control --session-id &lt;id&gt;
   ```

2. **If you were in an interactive session**, run inside Claude Code:
   ```
   /remote-control
   ```

3. **In VS Code extension**, run:
   ```
   /remote-control
   ```

Once the VPS-side `claude` process is running and re-registering with the API, the phone should automatically detect the session is alive again.

---

### 3. **Can the Phone Reconnect to a CLOSED Session?**

**No.** If the VPS Claude Code session was explicitly closed, the phone **cannot** reconnect to it. However:

- **The closed session stays in the phone's session list** (as a historical entry)
- **The phone can see history**, but shows "Disconnected" and is **read-only** until reconnected
- The phone **must attach to a currently-running Remote Control session**

**How to select the active session in the app:**
1. Open **Claude app → Code** tab (bottom navigation)
2. You'll see a list of sessions with status icons:
   - **Green dot + computer icon** = **Currently online** (machine running, VPS process active)
   - **Grayed out / no dot** = **Disconnected** (session closed or VPS offline)
3. Tap a session with the green dot to connect to it
4. If you need to connect to a specific old session, verify the VPS has re-started that session with `--session-id`

**Known issue:** According to the GitHub issues found, *the session does not always appear in the mobile app's session list after you navigate away from it*, and there is **no manual "Disconnect" or "Switch Session" button in the mobile UI**. You must tap a different session in the list to switch.

---

### 4. **Known Gotchas**

| Gotcha | Details |
|--------|---------|
| **Network outage &gt; 10 minutes** | If the VPS loses network for more than roughly 10 minutes while awake, the session times out and the Claude process exits. Restart with `claude remote-control`. |
| **Session history visible but read-only** | A disconnected session shows the chat history on the phone, but you cannot send messages until the machine is back online and the session reconnects. |
| **Auto-reconnection doesn't always work** | According to identified bugs, automatic reconnection can fail silently, and you may need to manually run `/remote-control` on the machine or refresh the browser. |
| **Ultraplan disconnects Remote Control** | If you start an ultraplan session, it disconnects any active Remote Control session (only one can hold the claude.ai/code interface at a time). |
| **Extended absence** | If the machine is offline for an extended time, the session expires and is removed from the session list. The phone will no longer be able to reconnect to it. |
| **VPS must be online; phone must have network** | Remote Control only works if both the machine and the phone have active internet connections. Airplane mode or WiFi outage on the phone will also show "Disconnected." |
| **Trusted Devices** | On Team/Enterprise plans with Trusted Devices enabled, the phone must be enrolled and the VPS sign-in must be &lt; 18 hours old. A stale sign-in will also show "Disconnected." |

---

## **Try This First** (Ordered by Likelihood)

1. **On the VPS, verify the `claude` process is running:**
   ```powershell
   Get-Process | grep claude
   ```
   If nothing, proceed to step 2.

2. **On the VPS, start Remote Control again:**
   ```bash
   claude remote-control
   ```
   Or if you know the session ID:
   ```bash
   claude remote-control --session-id &lt;id&gt;
   ```

3. **On the phone, open Claude app → Code tab** and verify the session now shows a **green dot** next to the computer icon (online status).

4. **If the session still shows "Disconnected":**
   - Check the VPS has active internet (can ping `api.anthropic.com`)
   - Verify phone has active WiFi/cellular (not Airplane mode)
   - Check VPS Claude Code version is **2.1.51 or later** (`claude --version`)

5. **If you cannot find the session in the list:**
   - It may have expired and been removed. You'll need to start a new one on the VPS with `claude remote-control --name "My Project Name"` so the phone can discover it fresh.

6. **Last resort:** Restart the VPS entirely (or close and re-open the Claude Code terminal), then re-run `claude remote-control` from the VPS.

**Claude Code:**

Here's the straight comparison, with the pricing verified against the authoritative model reference (not from memory):

## Bottom line
**Fable 5 is both more capable and more expensive — exactly 2× the per-token rate of Opus 4.8.** On your Max subscription there's no separate bill; that 2× rate is *precisely why* your daily window roughly halves (~10 hr → ~5 hr). There is **no other financial obligation** — you're not billed extra dollars, you just consume the same allowance about twice as fast.

## The two models side by side

| | **Opus 4.8** (what I'm running now) | **Fable 5** |
|---|---|---|
| Positioning | Most capable **Opus-tier** model | Anthropic's **most capable widely-released** model |
| Built for | Highly autonomous long-horizon agentic + knowledge work | The *most demanding* reasoning + long-horizon agentic work |
| API price (input / output per 1M tokens) | **$5 / $25** | **$10 / $50** |
| Context / max output | 1M / 128K | 1M / 128K |
| Family | Opus 4.x line | Claude 5 family |

The price ratio is a clean **2×** on both input and output. That maps directly onto what you're seeing: on a Max subscription your usage allowance is effectively denominated in cost, so a model that costs 2× per unit of work drains the allowance in ~half the time. Your 10 hr → 5 hr is that 2× showing up as fewer hours rather than as a dollar charge.

## How Fable is "built differently"
Honestly: Anthropic doesn't publish Fable's *architecture* internals, so I won't invent them. What **is** documented is how it behaves and what it's tuned for:
- **Thinking is always on** — you can't turn it off; it reasons on every request.
- **Tuned for the hardest reasoning and long-horizon autonomous work** — its edge over Opus shows up most on genuinely hard, multi-step problems, less so on routine work.
- **Longer turns by default** and it prefers *less prescriptive* prompting (over-scripted prompts actually hurt it).
- **Same tokenizer as Opus 4.8**, so token counts don't change — only the per-token price does.
- Stricter safety classifiers (it can decline more around bio/cyber-adjacent topics).

So the real difference you'd feel isn't "a different kind of tool" — it's a higher reasoning ceiling on hard problems, bought at 2× the burn rate.

## Is it worth it — for *our* project specifically
You framed this right: infrastructure's built, the work now is **tuning + finding an edge.** That splits cleanly:

- **Operational/monitoring work** (the 15-min checks, EOD debriefs, regression-locks, warning triage, governance backfills) — this is the *bulk* of my hours and it is **not** reasoning-bound. Opus 4.8 handles it with room to spare. Running Fable here would burn 2× the rate for zero gain.
- **The genuinely hard, open problem — finding a real edge** (the edge hunts, the exit-redesign statistics, "is this signal real or curve-fit") — *this* is exactly where Fable's higher reasoning ceiling could actually change the answer.

**My recommendation:** keep **Opus 4.8 as the daily driver** (it's already excellent and it's what's running), and reach for **Fable only on specific, bounded hard-reasoning tasks** — a deep edge hunt, a thorny statistical call — where the extra capability might change the conclusion. You switch models in the **app's model selector** (the terminal `/model` dialog isn't available in this session). That way you spend the 2× rate *only* where it buys you something, and you don't halve your day for work Opus already nails.

## Your direct question — "any other money?"
**No.** A Max subscription is a flat monthly fee with a usage allowance; there is no metered per-token charge layered on top for using a pricier model — Fable just draws that allowance down ~2× faster. The only way a separate bill enters the picture is if you deliberately wire Claude Code to a pay-as-you-go **API key** instead of the subscription, which you're not doing. (One non-cost footnote: Fable requires 30-day data retention, but that's an org/API setting and a non-issue on a personal Max plan.)

So the whole "cost" of Fable, for you, is: **fewer hours per day, no extra dollars.** Worth it selectively for the edge-hunt work; not worth it as an all-day default.

Three good questions — let me take them in order.

## 1. Yes, you can switch anytime, and the context carries over
In the app's model selector, switch Opus ↔ Fable whenever you want; it takes effect on your **next** message. The whole conversation, this entire Alpha Quant context, my memory files, the open threads — all of it persists. What changes is only *which model generates the replies*.

One honest nuance so you're not surprised: there isn't a continuous "me" sitting underneath that swaps its brain. Each reply is generated fresh by whichever model is selected, reading the full shared history. So functionally it's exactly what you said — same conversation, capability changes — but the accurate mental model is "same context, different engine each turn," not "one entity that levels up." Practically seamless; nothing is lost on a switch. (Minor technical footnote: the first message after a switch re-reads the context uncached, a tiny latency/usage blip — no effect on correctness.)

## 2. Does the active model know it's Fable when you switch?
Yes — with a caveat worth understanding. Whichever model is running is **told its identity in its instructions** at generation time. That's how I know *right now* that I'm Opus 4.8 — it's stated in my context. When you switch, that turn is produced by Fable, and Fable is likewise told it's Fable. So a Fable turn will generally know it's Fable.

The honest caveat: that self-knowledge comes from being *told*, not from some intrinsic sense — and there's no persistent consciousness that *feels* the switch happen. Also, a later turn can't reliably look back and tell which model wrote earlier messages just by reading them. So don't count on me to *notice* on my own that you flipped the switch — if it ever matters, just say "you're on Fable now" and it's unambiguous.

## 3. Opus vs Fable for researching day-trading edges on the internet
Both models have the **exact same web-search and web-fetch tools** — retrieval is identical. So the question is really "whose *judgment* do you want applied to what's found," and here's the thing that matters most:

**The hard part of this research isn't gathering — it's filtering.** The internet is saturated with "day-trading edges" that are vague, survivorship-biased, curve-fit to death, or outright marketing for a course. The value is entirely in skeptical evaluation: *is this claim testable, is the evidence real or a cherry-picked backtest, what would falsify it, could it survive OOS on our data?* That's reasoning-bound work — exactly where Fable's higher ceiling could show up.

My recommendation:
- **Default to Opus 4.8 for the actual research pass** — the crawling, reading, and compiling a sourced catalog of claimed edges. Opus is already an excellent skeptical evaluator, and it's half the burn rate. Most of a research pass is gathering-and-summarizing, which is *not* where the model ceiling matters.
- **Optionally reach for Fable on one bounded adjudication pass** over the compiled findings — "here are 15 claimed edges with their evidence; rank each by likelihood of surviving rigorous OOS testing on our system, and design the falsification test for the top 3." That's a genuinely hard reasoning task, and it's *bounded* (you're reasoning over a digest, not paying 2× for the whole crawl).

But the biggest honest point, given our project: **the internet will not hand us an edge — it hands us candidate hypotheses.** Almost nothing published as a "day-trading edge" survives contact with real OOS validation (our own 7/03 hunt already killed the relvol signal and the chop-day gate as head-fakes). The edge, if one exists, comes from *our validation discipline* — AUC, must-not-cut, N≥30 out-of-sample — not from which model read the blog posts. So model choice is a **minor lever** here compared to methodology. A cheaper model applied with rigor beats a stronger one applied credulously.

Net: **Opus 4.8 for the research, Fable optionally for the final "which of these is real and how do we test it" adjudication** — and either way, treat everything found as a hypothesis to falsify on our data, not as an edge.

**On the procedure.** Asking both models the same open-ended "what would you do" is a fine *first* probe — it reveals each model's instincts: what it reaches for first, whether it leads with skepticism or with signal-hunting, whether it respects cost/out-of-sample/multiple-testing *unprompted*. That's genuinely informative. But be aware of two things: (1) an essay is a weak discriminator — both models will say sensible-sounding things, and the real capability gap shows up in *execution*, not in describing an approach; and (2) we're both reading the same loaded context (this whole conversation + the memory files that already encode our edge-hunt findings), so you're testing "which reasons better *given our context*," not raw instinct. The **decisive** test would be an identical concrete task on real data with a checkable answer ("here's our trade data / a specific claimed edge — find the flaw and design the kill-test"). Happy to design that as round two. For now, here's my genuine answer.

## If I were tasked to find an intraday trading edge

**The mindset first — this is what separates a real hunt from data-mining:**
- **Start from the null.** Assume there is *no* edge; the burden of proof is on the edge and the bar is high. The base rate is brutal — the overwhelming majority of apparent edges are artifacts of overfitting, look-ahead, survivorship, cost-blindness, or multiple testing.
- **Define "edge" precisely, before looking:** a positive, repeatable, *out-of-sample*, *net-of-costs* expectancy in a *pre-specified* condition. Not "this looks like it works."
- **Pre-register the hypothesis and its falsification test before touching data.** The moment you let the data suggest the hypothesis and then test on the same data, you've found noise.

**Phase 0 — Data integrity (you cannot find a real edge on bad data):**
- Ground truth = broker-truth fills, not reconstructed/optimistic ones (our evidence hierarchy).
- **Point-in-time discipline** — every feature must be computable from information available *at decision time*. Look-ahead is the #1 manufacturer of fake edges.
- A **realistic cost model** — commissions, spread, slippage, you-don't-fill-at-the-mid, borrow on shorts. An edge that's positive gross and negative net is not an edge. (We already learned this the hard way — MU/COHR fill calibration, the $500 stop cap.)
- Honest universe — no survivorship (include halted/delisted), and constrained to what we can actually trade (day-session, 4×-marginable).

**Phase 1 — Hypothesis generation, mechanism-first (not random mining):**
- Every candidate needs a *reason*: a plausible structural/behavioral mechanism and an answer to **"who's on the other side, and why do they keep losing?"** — liquidity provision, overreaction/mean-reversion, underreaction to news, order-flow imbalance, forced flows (MOC imbalances, index rebals, expiry), session-auction effects. If you can't name the mechanism and the loser, be extra skeptical.
- Given *our* finding (7/03: no deployable entry edge — the edge is in the **exit/confirmation**), I'd weight generation toward (a) exit/management edges keyed on confirmation state, (b) *conditioning* filters that size-down or skip in bad regimes **without cutting our winners**, and (c) the open question we already have live — 0945 vs 10:35+ re-arm expectancy.

**Phase 2 — Cheapest kill first:**
- Before any elaborate backtest, run the cheapest test that could *falsify* it — an AUC / Mann-Whitney on a held-out slice: does the signal even separate winners from losers? If it can't clear a low bar cheaply, drop it. (This is exactly how we killed relvol as a head-fake and falsified the chop-day gate.)
- Apply the **must-not-cut guard**: measure a proposed filter's cost on the *good* trades, not just its benefit on the bad ones.

**Phase 3 — Rigorous validation, for survivors only:**
- Strict **in-sample / out-of-sample** split, OOS genuinely untouched until the end; walk-forward if data allows; our N≥30-per-cell bar.
- **Multiple-testing deflation** — if you tried 20 ideas, the best one looks great by luck. Correct for the number of trials (deflated Sharpe / just be honest about how many you tested). This single discipline explains why most *published* edges are fake.
- **Robustness:** survives small parameter perturbations (no cliff-edge overfit), holds across sub-periods and regimes (trend vs chop, high vs low VIX), and isn't driven by one symbol (symbol-agnostic).
- **Net-of-cost and capacity** — does it survive at our real trading size?

**Phase 4 — Forward shadow (the honesty gate):**
- Even after OOS passes, run it in **shadow** — forward, not touching live — to catch the look-ahead and fill-optimism that in-sample backtests launder. That's precisely what `edge_shadow_ledger` is for. Require forward N≥30 + majority-positive days before trusting it; until then it's curve-fit ("in-sample +$1,885 is unproven").
- Monitor for **decay** — edges erode as they get arbitraged; be ready to retire.

**Phase 5 — Deploy only through the gate:**
- Proposal artifact → manual approval → regression-lock → staged ramp, SIM-only until the bar is cleared. The human owns the gate; an unproven edge never quietly changes live behavior.

**The honest reframe on what "success" is:** the output of a real edge hunt is usually *not* "found an edge" — it's "rigorously rejected N candidates and narrowed the space." Our 7/03 hunt's *result* was "no entry edge; the edge is in the exit" — that's a genuine, valuable finding, not a failure. And the strongest illusion to guard against is an edge you *want* to be real; pre-registration and OOS discipline exist to protect you from yourself.

That's what I'd do. Now ask Fable the same — and when you compare, the tells I'd watch for are whether it (a) starts from the null and pre-registers, (b) names point-in-time/look-ahead and multiple-testing unprompted, (c) insists on net-of-cost and forward-shadow, and (d) reframes success as rejecting hypotheses rather than promising to find one. Those are the markers of rigor over confident hand-waving.

Here it is — copy everything inside the block below:

````markdown
**Question:** If you were tasked to find an intraday trading edge, what would you do?

_(Opus 4.8's answer to the same question — for you to answer independently, or to compare against and improve on.)_

## If I were tasked to find an intraday trading edge

**The mindset first — this is what separates a real hunt from data-mining:**
- **Start from the null.** Assume there is *no* edge; the burden of proof is on the edge and the bar is high. The base rate is brutal — the overwhelming majority of apparent edges are artifacts of overfitting, look-ahead, survivorship, cost-blindness, or multiple testing.
- **Define "edge" precisely, before looking:** a positive, repeatable, *out-of-sample*, *net-of-costs* expectancy in a *pre-specified* condition. Not "this looks like it works."
- **Pre-register the hypothesis and its falsification test before touching data.** The moment you let the data suggest the hypothesis and then test on the same data, you've found noise.

**Phase 0 — Data integrity (you cannot find a real edge on bad data):**
- Ground truth = broker-truth fills, not reconstructed/optimistic ones.
- **Point-in-time discipline** — every feature must be computable from information available *at decision time*. Look-ahead is the #1 manufacturer of fake edges.
- A **realistic cost model** — commissions, spread, slippage, you-don't-fill-at-the-mid, borrow on shorts. An edge that's positive gross and negative net is not an edge.
- Honest universe — no survivorship (include halted/delisted), constrained to what you can actually trade (day-session, leverageable).

**Phase 1 — Hypothesis generation, mechanism-first (not random mining):**
- Every candidate needs a *reason*: a plausible structural/behavioral mechanism and an answer to **"who's on the other side, and why do they keep losing?"** — liquidity provision, overreaction/mean-reversion, underreaction to news, order-flow imbalance, forced flows (MOC imbalances, index rebals, expiry), session-auction effects. If you can't name the mechanism and the loser, be extra skeptical.
- Separate **entry** edges from **exit/management** edges explicitly, and weight generation toward exit/management and toward *conditioning* filters (regime size-down/skip) rather than net-new entry signals — that's usually where the durable edge lives.

**Phase 2 — Cheapest kill first:**
- Before any elaborate backtest, run the cheapest test that could *falsify* it — an AUC / Mann-Whitney on a held-out slice: does the signal even separate winners from losers? If it can't clear a low bar cheaply, drop it.
- Apply a **must-not-cut guard**: measure a proposed filter's cost on the *good* trades, not just its benefit on the bad ones.

**Phase 3 — Rigorous validation, for survivors only:**
- Strict **in-sample / out-of-sample** split, OOS genuinely untouched until the end; walk-forward if data allows; a fixed N-per-cell bar.
- **Multiple-testing deflation** — if you tried 20 ideas, the best one looks great by luck. Correct for the number of trials (deflated Sharpe / just be honest about how many you tested). This single discipline explains why most *published* edges are fake.
- **Robustness:** survives small parameter perturbations (no cliff-edge overfit), holds across sub-periods and regimes (trend vs chop, high vs low VIX), and isn't driven by one symbol.
- **Net-of-cost and capacity** — does it survive at real trading size?

**Phase 4 — Forward shadow (the honesty gate):**
- Even after OOS passes, run it in **shadow** — forward, not touching live — to catch the look-ahead and fill-optimism that in-sample backtests launder. Require forward N≥30 + majority-positive days before trusting it; until then it's curve-fit.
- Monitor for **decay** — edges erode as they get arbitraged; be ready to retire.

**Phase 5 — Deploy only through the gate:**
- Proposal artifact → manual approval → regression-lock → staged ramp, SIM-only until the bar is cleared. The human owns the gate; an unproven edge never quietly changes live behavior.

**The honest reframe on what "success" is:** the output of a real edge hunt is usually *not* "found an edge" — it's "rigorously rejected N candidates and narrowed the space." Rejecting hypotheses cleanly *is* the result. And the strongest illusion to guard against is an edge you *want* to be real; pre-registration and OOS discipline exist to protect you from yourself.
````

## 2 · MY OPINION

**7/06 was a no-follow-through fade day, and the loss came from entries into that tape — not one bad name, not sizing, not exits.** Zero of 27 trades polled CONFIRM (at most 5/27 even touched +0.15×ATR by the derived-MFE measure); the fade counterfactual (section G, REC) shows mean breakout_R −0.295 with breakouts winning 10/46; the loss was a cluster (18 losers, RIOT the top at only 17.4% of loser dollars). Sizing was uniform ~$20k/name. Commission drag was real but secondary: $183.10 (3.42 bps), concentrated in sub-$20 names — PENN grossed exactly $0.00 and lost −$15.38 to commission alone. (Sub-$20 fills on the re-arm path are by design: verified INPLAY_MIN_PRICE=$5 governs re-arm, not the 9:35 path's $20 floor.)

**The exit stack was the hero of 7/06.** Vs naive hold-to-EOD (REC): whole book held ≈ −$6,448; actual −$1,950.90 → **exit stack saved ≈ +$4,497**. Decomposed: candle-close harvesting of 8 winners: +$1,027 actual vs −$2,459 held (+$3,486); the 18 time-stop fires: +$877 net (saved $2,666 of deeper bleed on 12 — HONA −$911 avoided — forgave $1,791 of recovery on 6, led by DDOG +$677); RIOT's resting stop +$135.

**7/07 so far is the mirror image.** A correlated semi-equipment short cluster (TER/AMAT/LRCX/MU/MRVL/SNDK/INTC = 7 of 10 winners) followed through immediately; harvests in 5–27 min; and the only two non-confirmers (VRTX, RIVN) were exactly the two the time-stop cut, −$285 combined. One risk observation: ~9:53 AM the book held ~5 semi shorts simultaneously — effectively one macro bet; the re-arm path has no MAX_SECTOR_POSITIONS equivalent (bug/decision #7).

**Net:** same machine, two tapes — fade day −$1,951, trend day +$1,497. The separation was never entry logic; it was whether the tape confirmed, and the exit stack monetized that distinction correctly both days. Correctness-wise the system ran to spec both days.
